details:
**Absheron Peninsula and Baku**
The Absheron Peninsula juts from Azerbaijan into the western Caspian and holds Baku, the lowest-lying national capital in the world at about 28 meters below sea level. Baku, the largest city on the Caspian, grew rich from offshore oil and is known for its Flame Towers skyscrapers. Azerbaijan also has more mud volcanoes than any other country, many of them protected in the Gobustan Reserve near Baku.

**Volga and Ural Rivers**
The two major rivers flowing into the Caspian from the north. The Volga, Europe's longest river, provides most of its inflow and ends in a large delta containing the city of Astrakhan. The Ural River is often used as a boundary between Europe and Asia.

**Alborz Mountains and Mount Damavand**
The Alborz range in northern Iran forms the Caspian's southern boundary and continues east toward the mountains of Khorasan. Its highest peak, the dormant volcano Mount Damavand, is the tallest mountain in Iran and one of the most topographically prominent peaks in Asia.

**Garabogazköl (Kara-Bogaz-Gol)**
A hypersaline lagoon on the Caspian's eastern shore in Turkmenistan, linked to the sea by a narrow strait and far saltier than the sea itself. It supports a salt and mineral industry, which Konstantin Paustovsky described in his 1932 book Kara-Bugaz.

**Beluga caviar and sturgeon**
The Caspian supplies the large majority of the world's wild caviar, most famously beluga caviar from the beluga sturgeon. Overfishing, poaching and pollution have left its sturgeon species critically endangered.

**Largest lake in the world**
Despite being called a "sea," the Caspian is the world's largest lake by surface area and holds roughly 40% of the world's lake water. It is endorheic, so it has no outflow except evaporation, and its water is brackish. It is a remnant of the ancient Tethys (Paratethys) Ocean. Its countries are Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan.

**Neft Daşları (Oil Rocks)**
An industrial settlement built on stilts and landfill in the Caspian off Azerbaijan, begun in 1949 as the world's first offshore oil platform. It grew into a town with housing, roads and workers' facilities far out at sea.

**Hyrcanian forests and Golestan National Park**
Ancient broadleaf forests along the southern Caspian coast in Iran's Gilan, Mazandaran and Golestan provinces. Golestan National Park holds one of the northernmost leopard populations. The now-extinct Caspian tiger was once a top predator in these forests.

**Turkmenbashi (formerly Krasnovodsk)**
A Turkmen port on the eastern Caspian. In 1993 the dictator Saparmurat Niyazov, who called himself "Turkmenbashi" ("leader of the Turkmen") and wrote the spiritual book Ruhnama, renamed the city after himself. Turkmenistan's capital, Ashgabat, is not on the coast.

**Ogurja Ada and other islands**
Ogurja Ada, off Turkmenistan, is the Caspian's largest island and part of the Hazar Nature Reserve. Other islands that come up are the Tyuleniy Archipelago, Chechen Island in the west, and Bulla Island off Azerbaijan.

**Caspian seal**
A small earless seal found only in the Caspian, one of the few seals that live in landlocked waters (like the Baikal seal). A mass die-off of thousands of Caspian seals on the Russian coast in late 2022 had no clear cause.

**Zebra mussel and native fauna**
The zebra mussel is native to the Ponto-Caspian region, where the Caspian was the center of its original range. It later became a major invasive species in Europe and North America. Other animals named for or native to the sea include the kutum fish and the Caspian (striped-neck) terrapin.

**Caspian Sea Monster**
The nickname Western intelligence gave to the KM, a huge Soviet ekranoplan (ground-effect vehicle) tested on the Caspian. It was a plane-like craft over 90 meters long, designed to skim just a few meters above the water.

**Nobel brothers and the Zoroaster**
Ludvig and Robert Nobel, brothers of Alfred Nobel, founded the Branobel oil company in Baku. In 1878 they launched the Zoroaster on the Caspian, often called the world's first successful oil tanker.

**Coastal cities and pipelines**
Besides Baku, cities on the coast include Atyrau and Aktau in Kazakhstan (which leads Caspian oil production), Derbent and Makhachkala in Russia, and Turkmenbashi in Turkmenistan. The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline carries Caspian oil to the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
